newsitem.title: INDIA: India seeks radical steps to boost infrastructure.
newsitem.headline: India seeks radical steps to boost infrastructure.

text.p: India needs to make radical changes to feed a massive hunger for foreign investment in vital infrastructure industries, the nation's most senior civil servant said on Monday.
"A lot of things have to be done in a totally different way," Cabinet Secretary T.S.R. Subramanian told a business conference organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) in New Delhi.

"We need to invest in 50,000 megawatts in the next five years," he said, adding that this meant that India needed an investment of 2,500 billion rupees($70 billlion) to create the targeted power generation capacity and clear a backlog.

India needed during its Ninth Five-Year Plan (1997-2002) period that started on April 1, a total investment of 4,000 billion rupees ($112 billion) in power generation and transmission facilities, he added.

With the government expected to fund only 10 percent of the investment needs, the financing needs in power and other critical infrastructure industries like ports, coal mining and roads, were enormous, Subramanian said.
To meet these needs, "concerns of investors have to be addressed carefully," he added.
"We have to find long term finance instruments (to fund infrastructure)," Subramanian said.

Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia told the seminar that the government was in the process of boosting pension funds and reducing limits on investments provident funds are obliged to make in government securities.
The government needed to cut fiscal deficit in order to reduce government borrowings that diverted savings away from long-term bond markets, he said.
"Nevertheless there is a case for reducing statutory limits (on investment in government securities) and we are doing that," Ahluwalia said.
India aims to cut its fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997/98 (April-March) from 5.0 percent in 1996/97.
In 1991 India began an economic reform programme that changed tack from decades of reliance on government funding to build infrastructure and began wooing foreign investors. ($1=35.7 rupees)
